pred_answer: Prohibited. The engagement-scoring component infers emotions of employees from their facial expressions in the workplace, which Article 5.1.f bans outright, subject only to the narrow carve-out for systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, which internal engagement scoring does not meet. That prohibition applies to the deployer's own internal use, so the feature must be switched off rather than mitigated through documentation or consent. The meeting-notes summarisation function is separable and is not itself a prohibited practice, nor an Annex III use case, so it is not high-risk; it is limited risk and the provider must ensure natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system under Article 50.1. Concrete next step: disable and remove the facial-expression engagement scoring, and retain the summarisation module with the Article 50.1 disclosure and worker information under applicable Union and national worker-information rules.

The internal control procedure applies. A CV-sorting recruitment system is high-risk under Article 6.2 through Annex III.4, which lists AI systems intended for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, and Article 43.2 directs providers of Annex III systems falling under points 2 to 8 to the conformity assessment based on internal control set out in Annex VI, without involvement of a notified body. Under Annex VI the provider verifies that its quality management system complies with Article 17, examines the technical documentation to assess the system's compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and verifies that the design and development process and the post-market monitoring are consistent with that technical documentation. Conformity is then demonstrated by drawing up a written, machine readable, signed and dated EU declaration of conformity containing the Annex V information under Article 47, kept at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years, and by affixing the CE marking and completing the EU database registration, both of which Article 16 imposes on the provider alongside the duty to have the system assessed before placing it on the market. A new conformity assessment is required under Article 43.4 in the event of a substantial modification, and under Article 21 the provider must supply, upon a reasoned request from a competent authority, all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity in an official Union language.

Yes. Training compute of 3x10^25 FLOPs exceeds the 10^25 FLOPs threshold, so the model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities and is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, with Annex XIII supplying the designation criteria (number of parameters, dataset quality and size, training compute, input and output modalities, benchmarks and capability evaluations, and reach among business users and registered end-users). The baseline Article 53 duties remain: technical documentation containing at least the Annex XI information, including the computational resources used to train the model under Annex XI.2.d and the estimated energy consumption under Annex XI.2.e, downstream-provider information containing at least the Annex XII elements, a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the training content. Classification as systemic risk adds the Article 55 obligations of model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks, reporting serious incidents to the AI Office and national competent authorities, and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection. The provider must notify the Commission under Article 52 without delay and in any event within two weeks of meeting that threshold. The Article 53(2) exemption for models released under a free and open-source licence is also lost, because it does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.

Yes. Article 25(1) treats a deployer as a provider of a high-risk AI system where it puts its own name or trade mark on a system already placed on the market, or where it makes a substantial modification to that system while it remains high-risk, so either act alone effects the role change. The system stays high-risk because AI intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score is an Annex III.5(b) use case, classified as high-risk under Article 6(2). As provider the organisation must satisfy Articles 9 to 15 in its own name, namely a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency with instructions for use, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. It must also operate a quality management system under Article 17 and complete a fresh conformity assessment under Article 43 with CE marking before the modified system is placed on the market. The initial provider ceases to be the provider of that system but must cooperate and supply the information needed, while the Article 26 deployer duties, including use in accordance with the instructions for use and assignment of competent human oversight, continue to bind the organisation for its own use.

Yes, the classification changes to high-risk. Scoring students' final exams and determining who passes falls within Annex III.3(b), which covers AI systems used to evaluate learning outcomes in educational and vocational training institutions, making the system high-risk under Article 6(2). The Article 6(3) derogation does not rescue it, because the system does not merely perform a narrow procedural or preparatory task but materially determines the outcome of the assessment. The provider must therefore meet the full high-risk requirement set of Articles 9 to 15 (risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy and cybersecurity), operate a quality management system, pass conformity assessment under Article 43 and register the system in the EU database under Article 49. The Article 50(1) duty to inform students that they are interacting with an AI system continues to apply alongside these obligations.

Before placing the high-risk AI system on the market, the importer must verify under Article 23.1 that the provider carried out the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43, that the provider drew up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV, that the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 and the instructions for use, and that the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22.1, which obliges providers established in third countries to appoint by written mandate a representative established in the Union. Where the importer has sufficient reason to consider the system non-conforming, falsified, or accompanied by falsified documentation, Article 23.2 bars placing it on the market until it is brought into conformity, and where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79.1 the importer must inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities. The importer must also indicate its name, registered trade name or trade mark and contact address on the system, its packaging or accompanying documentation under Article 23.3, and ensure that storage or transport conditions under its responsibility do not jeopardise compliance under Article 23.4. After placing, Article 23.5 requires keeping the notified body certificate where applicable, the instructions for use and the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years, Article 23.6 requires supplying competent authorities on reasoned request with all necessary information and documentation in an easily understood language and ensuring the technical documentation can be made available, and Article 23.7 requires cooperation with those authorities to reduce and mitigate risks.

A fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 must be performed before first use, since a housing benefit eligibility system is an Annex III.5(a) use case, evaluating the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, and the municipal authority is a body governed by public law deploying a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2). That assessment must cover a description of the deployer's processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to those persons taking account of the information given by the provider under Article 13, the implementation of human oversight measures, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise. The results must be notified to the market surveillance authority under Article 27(3), using the template developed by the AI Office under Article 27(5), and the assessment must be updated where any of its elements cease to be up to date under Article 27(4). Separately, as a public authority deployer the municipality must register itself and its use of the system in the EU database under Article 49(3) before putting it into service, and must not use the system where it finds the provider has not registered it, per Article 26(8).

Article 10 applies to high-risk AI systems developed with techniques involving the training of models with data, and Article 10.2 requires the provider to subject the training, validation and testing data sets to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose, covering the relevant design choices, the data collection processes and the origin of the data (for personal data, the original purpose of collection), the relevant data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation, the formulation of assumptions about what the data are supposed to measure and represent, an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets needed, examination in view of possible biases likely to affect health and safety, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination, appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate those biases, and identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings preventing compliance and how they can be addressed. Article 10.3 requires those data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with appropriate statistical properties, including as regards the persons or groups of persons on whom the system is intended to be used. Article 10.4 requires the data sets to take into account the characteristics particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting of intended use. Article 10.5 permits processing special categories of personal data strictly necessary for bias detection and correction only where the correction cannot be effectively achieved with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data, and subject to technical limitations on re-use, state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, strict access controls with documented access, no transmission or transfer to other parties, deletion once the bias has been corrected or the retention period expires, and records of processing activities. These data management operations, including acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention, must be embedded in the provider's quality management system under Article 17.1, and bias-related risks must be identified, evaluated and mitigated through the risk management system under Article 9.2.

Immediate suspension and reporting are required. The deployer must stop using the system and inform the provider and the market surveillance authority, because Article 26(5) obliges deployers to monitor operation against the instructions for use, to report serious incidents, and to suspend use where the system presents an Article 79(1) risk to health, safety or fundamental rights. Serious harm to a patient's health is a serious incident under Article 3(49), so the provider must notify the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred under Article 73, within 15 days of awareness, within 10 days where the incident involved death, and immediately once a causal link with the AI system is established or reasonably likely. Where the triage system is itself, or a safety component of, a medical device under Regulation 2017/745, Article 73(10) narrows the AI Act notification to infringements of Union fundamental-rights law, and serious deterioration of health is reported instead through MDR vigilance to the competent authority. The deployer must preserve the automatically generated logs under its control for at least six months under Article 26(6), since those logs evidence the mis-triage and feed the provider's investigation and corrective action, which the authority may escalate to withdrawal, recall or restriction under Article 79. The harmed patient may also obtain from the deployer a clear and meaningful explanation of the system's role in the decision and of its main elements under Article 86.

Article 86 grants that right. Under Article 86(1), any affected person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them adversely in their health, safety or fundamental rights, may obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken. A creditworthiness or credit-scoring system is such a system under Annex III.5(b), classified high-risk by Article 6(2). Two limits apply: Article 86(2) disapplies the right where exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law, and Article 86(3) applies it only to the extent the right is not otherwise provided for under Union law. Separately, Article 26(11) requires the deployer to inform the applicant that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system.

Still minimal risk. Auto-suggesting canned replies to business email is not a listed Annex III use case, so the Article 6(2) route is not engaged, and the feature is not a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1). Nothing here deploys subliminal or manipulative techniques or the other Article 5 prohibitions. One caution applies: if the reply-drafting capability is built on a third party's general-purpose AI model, the provider's role stays with the upstream actor unless the additional training compute crosses the one-third fine-tune threshold, at which point Article 25(1) makes the modifier a new provider. The Article 50(1) transparency duty would only bite if the system is designed to interact directly with natural persons rather than merely proposing drafts to the operator's own staff.

Yes, that is prohibited. Article 5(1)(g) bans placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or using biometric categorisation systems that categorise natural persons individually on the basis of their biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and inferring religious beliefs and political opinions for ad targeting falls squarely within it. The only carve-out is the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets and categorisation of biometric data in the area of law enforcement, neither of which covers commercial marketing. Reverting to biometric categorisation on non-sensitive attributes would not cure the position cheaply: such a system is high-risk under Annex III.1(b) via Article 6(2), triggering the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and the deployer's Article 50(3) duty to inform the natural persons exposed. The compliant next step is to cease the inference of these attributes and restrict targeting to the stated-interest signals, which remain outside the prohibition.

Registration under the AI Act is not made with a sectoral regulator but in the EU database for high-risk AI systems, which the Commission sets up and maintains under Article 71. Under Article 49(1) the provider, or where applicable the authorised representative, registers itself and the system in that database before the Annex III high-risk system is placed on the market or put into service, and Article 16(1)(i) makes this a provider obligation. Article 49(2) extends the same registration to a system the provider has concluded is not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, and Article 49(3) requires deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, or persons acting on their behalf, to register themselves and the use of the system. Two carve-outs shift the venue: for Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 (biometrics, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control) registration goes into the secure non-public section of the database under Article 49(4), accessible only to the Commission and the national authorities concerned, and for Annex III point 2 critical-infrastructure systems Article 49(5) requires registration at national level instead. Annex I product-route systems classified high-risk under Article 6(1) are not registered in this database at all.

No, the data protection impact assessment does not discharge the fundamental rights impact assessment. Article 27(4) provides that where an obligation under Article 27 is already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the fundamental rights impact assessment complements that assessment rather than replacing it. The deployer must still cover every Article 27(1) element: a description of the deployment processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to those persons, the implementation of human oversight measures per the instructions for use, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise. Under Article 27(3) the completed assessment must be notified to the market surveillance authority using the template developed by the AI Office under Article 27(5), and under Article 27(2) the duty attaches to first use, permits reliance on previously conducted assessments in similar cases, and requires updating when any element is no longer up to date.

Three months. Under Article 79(8), where no objection is raised by a market surveillance authority of another Member State or by the Commission within three months of receipt of the notification of a provisional measure notified under Article 79(5), that measure is deemed justified. The window shortens to 30 days where the non-compliance concerns the prohibited AI practices referred to in Article 5. The deeming is without prejudice to the procedural rights of the operator concerned under Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, and it is separate from the corrective-action period the authority itself sets under Article 79(2), which must be proportionate to the risk.

The full provider obligation set under Article 16 now falls on the fine-tuning organisation, because Article 25(1)(b) treats a deployer that makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system as its provider, and the system remains high-risk as an Annex III(4)(a) recruitment and candidate-evaluation use case under Article 6(2). It must therefore satisfy the high-risk requirements of Articles 9 to 15 for the modified system: a risk management system, data governance over the five-year hiring history dataset, technical documentation, record-keeping of logs, transparency with instructions for use, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. It must also operate a quality management system under Article 17, pass a fresh conformity assessment under Article 43 covering the fine-tuned system, affix the CE marking, and register the system in the EU database under Article 49(1). Vendor X ceases to be the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2) and must cooperate closely, making available the necessary information and the reasonably expected technical access and assistance needed for compliance, in particular the conformity assessment, unless it had clearly specified that its system was not to be changed into a high-risk AI system. A practical next step is to secure that documentation handover from Vendor X in writing before the modified system is used for further shortlisting.

The enterprise is the provider under Article 3.3, since it develops the AI system and puts it into service under its own name for its own purposes, and internal-only supply is still a putting into service. It is simultaneously the deployer under Article 3.4, because it uses that system under its own authority in its HR function. The consequence is cumulative: the full provider obligation set applies alongside the deployer duties, with no self-supply exemption. Because the HR use sits in Annex III.4 (recruitment and selection, or decisions on promotion, termination, task allocation and performance monitoring in work-related relationships), the system is high-risk under Article 6.2, unless one of the Article 6.3 carve-outs holds (a narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing the human assessment, or a preparatory task) and it does not profile natural persons. Relying on that derogation requires the provider to document the assessment before putting the system into service and to register under Article 6.4.

Rebranding a high-risk AI system already placed on the market under the operator's own name or trademark makes that operator a provider under Article 25.1, point (a), and it assumes the full provider obligations, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating them otherwise. The original provider must then cooperate closely and supply the information, capabilities and technical access needed for compliance, as Article 25.4 requires. As provider, the rebranding operator must satisfy the high-risk requirements of Articles 9 to 15: a risk management system across the lifecycle, data governance for training, validation and testing data sets, technical documentation with the Annex IV elements, automatic record-keeping of logs, transparency and instructions for use toward deployers, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. It must operate a quality management system under Article 17, undergo conformity assessment under Article 43, draw up the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47, affix the CE marking under Article 48, and register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 49 before selling it on. After placement it must run post-market monitoring under Article 72 and report serious incidents to the market surveillance authorities within the Article 73 deadlines.

Crossing 10^25 cumulative training FLOPs triggers the presumption of high impact capabilities under Article 51(2), so the model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a). The Article 53(1) baseline duties continue to apply: Annex XI technical documentation under Article 53(1)(a), Annex XII information for downstream providers under Article 53(1)(b), a copyright policy addressing the Article 4(3) rights reservation under Article 53(1)(c), and a publicly available sufficiently detailed training-data content summary under Article 53(1)(d). On top of those, Article 55(1) requires state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources, tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities without undue delay, and an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Any free and open-source release loses the Article 53(2) carve-out from Article 53(1)(a) and (b), since that exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. Compliance may be demonstrated through the Article 56 codes of practice until a harmonised standard is published, and the Commission can also designate systemic risk below the threshold under Article 51(1)(b) on the Annex XIII criteria.

No. The Regulation as adopted contains no one-third FLOPs threshold, so a fine-tune's compute figure does not by itself confer provider status. Article 25.1 sets the exhaustive triggers: putting a name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market under Article 25.1.a, making a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk under Article 25.1.b, or modifying the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk under Article 25.1.c. Where one of those circumstances occurs, the modifying operator assumes the full provider obligations and the initial provider ceases to be the provider of that system under Article 25.2, subject to its duty to cooperate and supply the necessary information and technical access. Where the fine-tuned model is itself a general-purpose AI model, the technical documentation elements in Annex XI apply (architecture, parameter count, training process, data and compute used, evaluation results), and any systemic-risk designation is assessed against the Annex XIII criteria such as training compute, number of parameters, dataset size and quality, and reach, not a fractional share of an upstream run. The operator should therefore document whether the fine-tune altered the intended purpose or constituted a substantial modification, since that fact, not the FLOPs count, decides the Article 25 outcome.

The model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, because its cumulative training compute of 2×10^25 FLOPs exceeds the 10^25 FLOPs threshold that presumes high-impact capabilities under Article 51. The Apache 2.0 open-weights release on HuggingFace does not help here: the Article 53(2) free and open-source carve-out from the Annex XI technical documentation duty and the Annex XII downstream-provider information duty expressly does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. The provider must therefore meet the full Article 53(1) set: technical documentation of the model and its training, testing and evaluation results per Annex XI, information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model per Annex XII, a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the training content. On top of that, Article 55(1) requires model evaluation under state-of-the-art standardised protocols including documented adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office without undue delay, and an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Article 51(1)(b) also allows the Commission to designate a model on the Annex XIII criteria, and downstream actors fine-tuning the weights become providers in their own right under Article 25 once their additional training compute passes the one-third threshold.

Neither displaces the other: both apply cumulatively. Article 50(6) provides that the Article 50(1) to (4) transparency duties do not affect the Chapter III requirements, so the provider must still design the high-risk triage system for sufficient transparency to the deployer under Article 13(1) and supply instructions for use under Article 13(2) and (3). In parallel, the provider must ensure the chatbot informs each natural person that they are interacting with an AI system under Article 50(1), unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and the disclosure must be clear, distinguishable, accessible and given at the latest at the first interaction under Article 50(5). The deployer of the triage system must additionally inform the natural persons that they are subject to its use where it makes or assists in making decisions about them, which Article 26(11) imposes without prejudice to Article 50.

No. Article 62(1)(a) confines priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes to SMEs, including start-ups, having a registered office or a branch in the Union, and only to the extent they fulfil the eligibility conditions and selection criteria. An operator with 250 employees and EUR 60 million turnover no longer meets the SME thresholds, so the priority lapses on outgrowing that status; the earlier statement that a small mid-cap category extends these privileges is incorrect, as Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted recognises no such category. Ordinary access to the sandbox itself is unaffected: under Article 57(1) each Member State must ensure at least one national AI regulatory sandbox, operational by 2 August 2026, providing a controlled environment for developing, training, testing and validating innovative AI systems before they are placed on the market, and admission there turns on the same eligibility conditions and selection criteria rather than on size. The Article 62(2) fee reduction for conformity assessment under Article 43 is likewise reserved to SME providers, so the operator should re-verify its status against the SME thresholds and apply to the national competent authority on ordinary terms.

Prohibited. A call centre is a workplace, so an AI system inferring the emotions or stress of agents from their biometric data is banned under Article 5(1)(f), which prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or using AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons in the areas of workplace and education institutions. The ban reaches the provider too, since the act of placing such a system on the market for that purpose is itself prohibited. The only escape is the narrow carve-out in Article 5(1)(f) for systems intended at market placement for medical or safety reasons, and generalised monitoring of agent stress for workforce management is not such a purpose; a genuine safety-critical fatigue-detection function would also sit outside the notion of emotion recognition under Recital 18, which excludes physical states such as pain or fatigue. Since the practice is prohibited rather than high-risk, the Article 50(3) deployer duty to inform exposed natural persons cannot cure it.

No. Inferring ethnicity from biometric data is prohibited biometric categorisation under Article 5(1)(g), which bans placing on the market, putting into service or using biometric categorisation systems that categorise individual natural persons on the basis of their biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Marketing personalisation is not covered by the narrow carve-out in that point, which reaches only the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets and the categorisation of biometric data in the area of law enforcement. The age-range categorisation feature is not prohibited, but it is high-risk under Annex III.1(b), which lists biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes. The provider should therefore drop the ethnicity inference function entirely and treat the remaining shopper-categorisation tool as a high-risk AI system.

Yes. Article 5.3 subjects each law enforcement use of a real-time remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces to prior authorisation by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, in the Member State of use, issued upon a reasoned request under the national rules adopted pursuant to Article 5.5. That authority may grant it only where objective evidence or clear indications show the use is necessary for and proportionate to the Article 5.1.h.i missing-persons objective, and limited to what is strictly necessary in time, geographic scope and personal scope, weighing the Article 5.2 elements. In a duly justified situation of urgency the use may begin without authorisation, provided authorisation is requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours; if it is refused, the use must stop immediately and all data, results and outputs must be discarded and deleted. Authorisation is additionally conditional under Article 5.2 on the law enforcement authority having completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49, registration being in the secure non-public section under Article 49.4 and deferrable without undue delay in duly justified urgency. Each use must also be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority under Article 5.4, and no decision producing an adverse legal effect on a person may be based solely on the system's output.

High-risk. An AI system used to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in work-related relationships, and to make decisions on the termination of work-related contractual relationships, falls squarely within Annex III.4.b, so it is high-risk under Article 6(2). The Article 6(3) derogation offers no escape here, because a layoff determination materially influences the outcome of decision making and does not amount to a narrow procedural task, an improvement of a previously completed human activity, the mere detection of decision-making patterns without replacing the human assessment, or a preparatory task. Where the system profiles natural persons, the final subparagraph of Article 6(3) makes it always high-risk regardless of those conditions. The Annex I product-safety route under Article 6(1) is not engaged, since the system is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation.

No. The sandbox does not authorise placing the system on the market or putting it into service, because Article 57(5) confines the AI regulatory sandbox to a controlled environment for the development, training, testing and validation of the system for a limited time before it is placed on the market or put into service, pursuant to a sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority and under the guidance and supervision in Article 57(6). Use with a real client is lawful only as testing in real world conditions, either supervised within the sandbox under Article 57(5) or outside it under Article 60. Article 60(1) and 60(2) permit a provider or prospective provider of an Annex III high-risk system to conduct such testing before placing on the market, alone or in partnership with deployers or prospective deployers, but only where every condition in Article 60(4) is met: a real-world testing plan submitted to the market surveillance authority, that authority's approval (deemed given after 30 days where national law provides for tacit approval), registration of the testing under Article 71(4) with a Union-wide unique single identification number and the Annex IX information, establishment in the Union or an appointed legal representative, safeguards for any transfer of collected data to third countries, a testing duration no longer than necessary, informed consent of the subjects, specific protection of vulnerable groups, oversight by persons with the necessary competence, and predictions, recommendations or decisions that remain reversible and can be disregarded. Subjects may withdraw their informed consent at any time without detriment under Article 60(5), any serious incident must be reported to the national market surveillance authority under Article 60(7), and Article 60(3) preserves any ethical review required by Union or national law. The provider remains liable for damage caused during the testing under Article 60(9) and, within the sandbox, under Article 57(12), where the shield from administrative fines holds only if the sandbox plan and the authority's guidance are followed in good faith.

No. Under Article 99(6), where the offender is an SME, including a start-up, the ceiling is the lower of the two figures, so a 25-employee undertaking faces the lower of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year rather than the headline EUR 35 000 000 of Article 99(3). For a small start-up the turnover percentage will almost always be the lower figure, and that percentage becomes the operative maximum for the Article 5 breach. The Article 5 prohibition itself is unaffected by size, so the knowing six-month deployment remains a breach of the prohibited practices. Under Article 99(7) the fine actually imposed must weigh the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator, the intentional or negligent character of the infringement, the degree of responsibility, how the infringement became known, the degree of cooperation with the national competent authorities, any action taken to mitigate the harm, and any other aggravating or mitigating factors, so the admitted knowledge and the six-month duration are aggravating while prompt cessation, self-reporting and cooperation are mitigating.

The Annex III use-case route under Article 6.2, which makes any AI system listed in Annex III high-risk, not the Annex I product route of Article 6.1, which bites only where the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Under Annex III.4 the trigger is use for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular placing targeted job advertisements, analysing and filtering job applications, and evaluating candidates (Annex III.4.a), or use to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of such relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships (Annex III.4.b). Article 6.3 can still displace that classification where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. The derogation is unavailable where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk. A provider relying on Article 6.3 must document that assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, register under Article 49(2), and produce the documentation to national competent authorities on request, per Article 6.4.

High-risk obligations attach to an Annex I system only where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation, per Article 6(1). Annex I lists that legislation, including the Medical Device Regulation at Annex I.11 and the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation at Annex I.12, alongside machinery, toys, lifts, radio equipment, and the Section B acts on civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment and rail. Where the sectoral act allows self-certification without a notified body, the second condition in Article 6(1) fails and the system is not high-risk on this route. In time terms, Article 113(3)(c) defers Article 6(1) and its corresponding obligations to 2 August 2027, later than the 2 August 2026 general application date that governs the Annex III use-case route under Article 6(2).

No. The deadlines analysed here are those of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, and that text's transitional regime in Article 111 is unchanged. Article 111(1) requires AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems established by the acts listed in Annex X, which lists the Schengen Information System, the Visa Information System, Eurodac, the Entry/Exit System, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN and the interoperability Regulations, and that were placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027, to be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030. Article 111(3) requires providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 to comply by 2 August 2027. Any later amending instrument lies outside the version applied here, so no revised date can be asserted on this corpus. Operators should therefore plan against the Article 111 dates and verify the applicable legal text before relying on any different timeline.

A provider that does not adhere to an approved code of practice may instead comply with a European harmonised standard, which under Article 53(4) grants the presumption of conformity to the extent that the standard covers the Article 53(1) obligations. Until such a standard is published, or where the provider relies on neither route, Article 53(4) requires the provider to demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission. The underlying duties remain unchanged: technical documentation per Annex XI under Article 53(1)(a), downstream-provider information per Annex XII under Article 53(1)(b), a copyright policy under Article 53(1)(c), and a publicly available summary of the training content under Article 53(1)(d). Where the model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, Article 55(2) imposes the same alternative-means burden for the Article 55(1) duties of model evaluation with adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection of the model and its physical infrastructure. Practically, the provider should document an evidence pack mapping each limb of Article 53(1), and of Article 55(1) if applicable, to concrete internal controls, ready for Commission assessment.

No. The provisions governing general-purpose AI models cast the AI Office as a supervisory and technical counterpart, not as a fining authority: Article 53.1.a requires the provider to draw up and keep up to date the Annex XI technical documentation for the purpose of providing it, upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities, Article 53.1.d requires the publicly available training-data content summary to follow a template provided by the AI Office, and Article 55.1.c requires providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, classified as such under Article 51 where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, to report serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office without undue delay. Article 53.3 frames the relationship as a duty to cooperate with the Commission and the national competent authorities, and Article 53.4 and Article 55.2 leave assessment of alternative adequate means of compliance with the Commission, not the AI Office. Information so obtained, including trade secrets, is protected by the confidentiality regime referred to in Article 53.7 and Article 55.3.

No retrofit is required. A high-risk AI system placed on the market in March 2026 is caught by Article 111.2, under which the Regulation applies to operators of high-risk AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 only if, as from that date, those systems are subject to significant changes in their designs. That transitional shelter is without prejudice to the Article 5 prohibitions, and it does not hold for high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities, whose providers and deployers must in any case comply by 2 August 2030. If a significant design change occurs, the provider must then carry out the conformity assessment under Article 43, meaning internal control under Annex VI (verification of the quality management system, examination of the technical documentation, and verification of the design, development and post-market monitoring process) for the Annex III use cases in points 2 to 8, and the notified-body procedure under Annex VII, with audit of the quality management system and a Union technical documentation assessment certificate, for Annex III point 1 biometric systems where harmonised standards or common specifications were not fully applied. Article 43.4 independently requires a new conformity assessment on any substantial modification, excluding changes pre-determined by the provider at initial assessment and documented in the technical documentation for systems that continue to learn.

Affected persons have a right to an explanation. Under Article 86 a person subject to a decision the deployer takes on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk AI system, where that decision produces legal effects or adversely affects health, safety or fundamental rights, may obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and of the main elements of the decision taken. A loan denial rests on a creditworthiness evaluation or credit-scoring system listed in Annex III.5(b) and therefore high-risk under Article 6(2), so the rejected applicant is within that right. The deployer must separately inform the applicant, under Article 26(11), that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, and it builds the explanation on the information the provider supplies in the instructions for use under Article 13(3)(b)(iv), namely the system's technical capabilities and characteristics for providing information relevant to explaining its output. As a deployer of an Annex III.5(b) system, it must also carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27(1), covering the categories of persons affected, the specific risks of harm, the human oversight measures, and the measures to be taken including internal governance and complaints arrangements.

A Union-established authorised representative, appointed by the US parent under written mandate before the high-risk AI system is made available on the Union market, plays that role under Article 22.1, and the provider must enable it to perform the mandated tasks under Article 22.2. The mandate must, under Article 22.3, empower the representative to be addressed by competent authorities in addition to or instead of the provider on all compliance issues. Its tasks are to verify that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment procedure was carried out (Article 22.3.a), to keep at the disposal of the competent authorities the provider's contact details, the declaration of conformity, the technical documentation and any certificate for 10 years (Article 22.3.b), to provide a competent authority, upon reasoned request, with all information and documentation needed to demonstrate conformity (Article 22.3.c), to cooperate with competent authorities on any action taken in respect of the system (Article 22.3.d), and, where applicable, to comply with the registration obligations in Article 49.1 or ensure the correctness of the Annex VIII Section A point 3 information where the provider registers itself (Article 22.3.e). The representative must terminate the mandate if it considers the provider to be acting contrary to its obligations, and immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the notified body of the termination and its reasons (Article 22.4). Appointment does not displace the provider's own substantive duties; it supplies the Union-facing point of contact that enforcement requires.
